chapter_theme: Conduct is to be guarded above life itself. It is what high birth really consists of, it outranks study, and its final test is living in accord with the world.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: conduct's excellence (131-132), the good that comes with it and the harm of its absence (133-137), its later results (138), and all conduct in speech and action summarised (139-140).

131.reading: Since conduct gives excellence, conduct is to be guarded more than life.
131.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reasoning is careful: life is the best of all things, but it doesn't confer distinction the way conduct does, so conduct gets greater care. He adds that this holds for high and low alike.

132.reading: Guard conduct with great effort; however much you search and weigh, it alone is the help.
132.nuance: The three forms of ஓம்பி, தெரிந்து and தேர்ந்து make it sound like a long investigation with one result. Parimelazhagar makes it a survey of all virtues, of which only this one helps in both lives.

133.reading: Having conduct is what noble birth is, and failing in it becomes low birth.
133.nuance: The verse redefines birth by behaviour. Even the conservative commentators allow that one's status can really change, though for Parimelazhagar it is within a varna frame that the verse doesn't state.

positions.position: Status really changes: a low-born person of good conduct becomes high, and a high-born person who fails falls.
positions.quote: உயர்ந்த வருணத்துப் பிறந்தாராயினும் ஒழுக்கத்தில் தவறத் தாழ்ந்த வருணத்தராவர்

positions.position: Conduct is the evidence of good birth, and failures are regarded as low-born whoever they are.
positions.quote: ஒழுக்கம் தவறுகிறவர்கள் யாவராயினும் அவர்கள் இழிந்த குடியில் பிறந்தவர்களாகவே கருதப்படுவர்.

134.reading: Even if forgotten, the Veda can be learned again, but a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct declines.
134.nuance: This is a pointed ranking, because study is what the Brahmin is supposed to be defined by. It makes birth a thing that can be lost. Parimelazhagar says the rule extends from this high example to the other varnas.

135.reading: As there is no prosperity in the envious, so there is no elevation in one who lacks conduct.
135.nuance: The simile takes as given what chapter 17 has yet to argue, that envy destroys wealth. Parimelazhagar uses verse 166 to extend it: as an envious man's kin suffer, so do a person's kin when conduct fails.

136.reading: The strong don't slacken in conduct, knowing what harm arises from a lapse.
136.nuance: The motive given is prudence, not love of virtue. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar differ a little on உரவோர், as strength of mind and understanding respectively, the same question raised by உரன் in verse 24.

137.reading: From conduct people attain high standing, and from lapses they attain blame not properly theirs.
137.nuance: எய்தாப் பழி is the sharp part. Parimelazhagar sees that after one slip, even a false charge from an enemy is believed. Conduct is therefore a shield as well as a good.

positions.position: When enemies make false charges, the world believes them because of the earlier lapse.
positions.quote: பகை பற்றி அடாப்பழி கூறியவழி, அதனையும் இழுக்கம்பற்றி உலகம் அடுக்கும் என்று கொள்ளுமாகலின்,

138.reading: Good conduct is a seed of good, and bad conduct always gives suffering.
138.nuance: The two halves are asymmetrical: one is a seed with a future harvest, the other suffers 'always'. Parimelazhagar shows each half implies what the other leaves out. Manakkudavar makes the seed one of release, which the verse doesn't say.

139.reading: Speaking evil with their mouths, even by a slip, is not possible for those who have conduct.
139.nuance: It's a strong claim: conduct has become so ingrained that the slip itself can't occur. Parimelazhagar adds speech improper to one's varna to the list of evil words, which is his addition. He also says the redundant 'with the mouth' implies that it's a mouth used to good words.

140.reading: Those who haven't learned to live in accord with the world have studied much and still lack understanding.
140.nuance: All three commentators narrow உலகம் to the noble. Yet Parimelazhagar makes an unusual concession in explaining why the verse says 'world': scripture contains things that no longer suit the present, and it omits things that do.

positions.position: Living with the world includes setting aside what the moral texts say that doesn't suit this age, and taking up what suits it.
positions.quote: அறநூல் சொல்லியவற்றுள் இக்காலத்திற்கு ஏலாதன ஒழிந்து, சொல்லாதனவற்றுள் ஏற்பன கொண்டு வருதலான்

links.note: The two ask the same question, what learning is worth, and answer differently. For 2, learning lacks fruit without worship, and for 140 it isn't understanding without fitting conduct in the world. One looks up and the other looks out.
131 places conduct above life in general. 327 gives a specific case: don't take another's life, even at the cost of your own. It shows what 'guarding it above life' can literally mean.

Both separate social rank from worth. 133 says this of conduct and birth, and 973 goes further with the high who aren't high and the low who aren't low. Read together, they show a repeated Kural challenge to status by birth.
Both tie understanding to how the world lives. Verse 426 calls it அறிவு to live as the world lives, which is a striking statement beside Parimelazhagar's narrowing of 'world' to the noble in 140.

source_issues: The Tamil of verse 134 in kg/core has a stray space, பார் ப்பான், and Pope's gloss there has 'bi rth'.
